To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the D-enantiomer content of aspartic acids in dentine increases linearly with age, at a rate which can be calibrated by the age of the individual, and which can be used to determine the age of the mammal.

aspartic acid residues in the stable proteins of teeth and other hard tissues undergo slow racemization over geological time and that the rate of racemization is proportional to the temperature at which the material is stored.

aspartic acid is a suitable amino acid for age determination in mammals because it undergoes racemisation in the body, and that dentine is more reliable than enamel as a source of aspartic acids for such determination because of the lower degree of attrition and the greater amount of material available.

the use of the D-aspartyl residue as an indicator of age in mammalian tissue.
the use of aspartic racemisation in proteins to determine the age of an organism.
